entries.title: Grounded knowledge assistant with retrieval-augmented generation
entries.summary: A standard RAG pattern pairs an application orchestrator with indexed source material so answers can be grounded in retrieved passages.

reference.title: Design and Develop a RAG Solution on Azure
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; no source image or wording reproduced.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Users need answers based on private or domain-specific documents that a general language model might not know. A fixed retrieval pipeline is a useful starting point for single-index question answering.

### Flow and Azure mapping
An editor or source system supplies documents; an ingestion pipeline chunks and enriches them, creates embeddings, and writes an Azure AI Search index. A user sends a question through an application API; an orchestrator retrieves relevant passages, builds a grounded prompt, calls a selected model endpoint, and returns a response with citations. Keep ingestion and query paths distinct in the diagram.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
Chunking, embedding choice, retrieval mode, access filtering, and evaluation are workload-specific and require testing. This is standard RAG, not agentic retrieval, and no response-quality guarantee is implied. Model deployment choice, private networking, identity filtering, and content safety are explicit follow-up decisions.

Source: [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/ai-ml/guide/rag/rag-solution-design-and-evaluation-guide).
caveats: Index access must enforce the caller's document permissions; the source emphasizes evaluation, not automatic correctness.

### Problem
Factories need interoperable collection and analysis of equipment telemetry across sites, including local edge processing and cloud insight workflows.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Industrial controllers and sensors expose OPC UA data to an edge environment running Azure IoT Operations on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes. Edge data flows normalize or filter telemetry, then deliver selected records through an Azure Event Hubs-compatible ingestion path to Azure Data Explorer or a Fabric eventhouse for query and dashboards. A distinct optional branch can send events to alerting or maintenance workflows.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The source solution uses a specific demonstration and includes Azure IoT Operations, PostgreSQL, and analytics options; this catalog diagram is a smaller conceptual abstraction, not a deployment reproduction. Site connectivity, OPC UA certificate trust, buffering, schema governance, and industrial safety remain design requirements. Do not depict cloud analytics as a replacement for deterministic control loops.

Source: [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/iot/iot-industrial-solution-architecture).

entries.title: Private machine-learning inference with controlled model promotion
entries.summary: A separated Dev, Stage, and Prod architecture trains candidate models, promotes versioned artifacts, and serves online inference privately.

reference.title: Baseline Azure Machine Learning Inference Reference Architecture
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; no source diagram or prose copied.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Enterprise ML teams need a controlled path from experimentation to production inference, with environment isolation, private access, and traceable model artifacts.

### Flow and Azure mapping
A Dev environment reads governed training data, runs feature preparation and training, evaluates a candidate, and publishes approved model and environment versions to a shared Azure Machine Learning registry. Promotion pipelines import the approved artifacts into Stage and Prod. AKS hosts online endpoints behind Application Gateway and API Management; private endpoints, managed identities, and monitoring support operations. Blue/green deployment shifts traffic only after validation.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Microsoft baseline is explicitly single-region and focuses on online inference; streaming inference is out of scope. The diagram should not imply that batch scoring, high availability, a particular feature store, or a full MLOps control framework is automatically included. Release gates and approval roles are conceptual, and must be designed for the organization's governance needs.

Source: [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/ai-ml/architecture/baseline-azure-machine-learning-inference).
caveats: Source architecture is single-region; a separate regional recovery design is required.

entries.title: Multi-region web application recovery with active-active routing
entries.summary: Identical independent web deployments serve through Azure Front Door, with health-based traffic exclusion when a region is impaired.

reference.title: Multiple-region Architectures for Azure App Service Disaster Recovery
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; no source diagram or prose copied.

supporting_sources.title: Two zones or three? A design framework for zone-resilient Azure workloads
supporting_sources.relevance: Clarifies that availability-zone protection is component-specific and does not replace a separate multi-region recovery design.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A single-region web application can become unavailable during a regional outage even when its regional deployment is otherwise highly available.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Deploy independent, equivalent App Service plans and web apps in two regions. Azure Front Door distributes normal traffic across both origins and uses health probes to stop routing to an impaired origin. Restrict direct public app access so requests traverse the edge entry point. Keep application state in suitable external data services and deploy configuration consistently through repeatable CI/CD.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
Active-active costs more and requires both regions to be ready for normal load and failover load. Data replication, consistency, session handling, and failback behavior are not solved by the web tier alone. The reference compares active-active, active-passive, and passive-cold options; this specific candidate selects active-active for exploration and makes no RTO/RPO promise. A database or storage layer needs its own recovery design.

Source: [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/web-apps/guides/multi-region-app-service/multi-region-app-service).
caveats: State replication and failover must be selected independently; Front Door health routing alone does not provide application-data recovery.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Organizations may need local workload execution and storage while using Azure for centralized governance, monitoring, security, and lifecycle management.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Validated physical machines connect through redundant top-of-rack switches and an upstream corporate network. The Azure Local instance provides Hyper-V and Storage Spaces Direct; workloads run as VMs or supported Kubernetes deployments. Azure Arc connects the instance to Azure management services, while Azure Monitor, Key Vault, Defender for Cloud, and backup/recovery services remain cloud-hosted. Management traffic and workload traffic should be distinguished from the local east-west storage path.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The source describes a connected, storage-switched baseline for 2–16 machines; it excludes single-machine, disconnected, switchless, rack-aware, and disaggregated designs. Hardware validation, networking, update cadence, and workload sizing are prerequisites. Do not depict Azure monitoring or policy agents as on-premises services unless the selected configuration explicitly supports that deployment.

Source: [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/hybrid/azure-local-baseline).

entries.title: Mainframe change-data capture into Azure analytics and serving stores
entries.summary: A change capture path moves mainframe or midrange updates over private connectivity into Azure event, database, and analytics targets.

reference.title: Replicate Mainframe Data by Using Precisely Connect
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; source architecture includes a commercial third-party replication product not reproduced in this candidate.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Modernization and analytics programs often need timely copies of legacy records while avoiding repeated heavy reads against operational mainframe systems.

### Flow and Azure mapping
A source-side capture component reads transaction logs and stages changes. A replication service transports ordered change records across ExpressRoute or VPN to an Azure landing point. Azure Event Hubs can carry streaming updates; downstream consumers can materialize selected records into Azure SQL or land them in Data Lake Storage/OneLake for analytics. A mapping and validation layer adapts source formats and schemas before consumer use.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Microsoft reference uses Precisely Connect for source capture, transport, and apply; Azure services alone do not automatically provide native mainframe log capture. This conceptual Azure-ready diagram therefore shows a generic, replaceable CDC connector as an external/partner component and highlights data consistency, schema conversion, initial-load coordination, replay, and source-system load as design decisions. It does not claim zero latency or exactly-once semantics.

Source: [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/example-scenario/mainframe/mainframe-replication-precisely-connect).

entries.title: Live digital twin graph for facilities and connected assets
entries.summary: A modeled twin graph combines device and business-system updates, supports relationship queries, and routes state changes to downstream analytics.

reference.title: What is Azure Digital Twins?
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; no source image or prose copied.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A facilities or asset team needs context-rich views of connected things and their relationships, rather than isolated device readings.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Model the domain with Digital Twins Definition Language and create twins and relationships in Azure Digital Twins. IoT Hub or other business-system connectors deliver property changes; Azure Functions can apply domain logic and keep the graph current. Queries traverse the graph for current operational context. Event routes can send changes through Event Grid, Event Hubs, or Service Bus to Azure Data Explorer or a downstream application. A 3D visualization is optional and should be shown as a consumer, not as the twin store.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
This differs from the industrial telemetry candidate: its focus is the contextual graph and topology, not OPC UA collection or edge operations. The twin is a model of real assets, not a replacement for the source of truth in every business system. Model evolution, event ordering, historical retention, and synchronization policies need explicit ownership.

Source: [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/digital-twins/overview).

entries.title: Cross-cloud and streaming analytics estate on Microsoft Fabric
entries.summary: Multiple cloud and on-premises sources feed Fabric lakehouse, warehouse, and event analytics with governance and BI consumers.

reference.title: Analytics End-to-End with Microsoft Fabric
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; the source uses third-party product names only as source examples; no provider diagram or wording copied.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
An organization has structured, unstructured, and streaming data spread across on-premises systems, Azure databases, and external cloud stores, and needs consistent analytics and reporting.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Use Fabric Data Factory copy/orchestration and database mirroring where supported, and eventstreams for real-time ingestion. OneLake provides the shared data layer; a lakehouse retains raw and semi-structured data, a warehouse serves structured SQL analytics, and an eventhouse handles high-volume event queries. Notebooks, Dataflow Gen2, or SQL transformations prepare curated datasets; Power BI and approved data/AI applications consume them. Microsoft Purview, Entra ID, and Key Vault are cross-cutting governance and identity services.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
This candidate is purposefully a cross-cloud ingestion and multi-modal analytics pattern, not the existing generic Fabric starter or Azure data warehouse. Connector availability, replication support, licensing, data residency, and source egress are workload-specific. Fabric and OneLake are a platform choice, not a claim that external stores are copied or federated automatically.

Source: [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/example-scenario/dataplate2e/data-platform-end-to-end).

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A mobile application needs user authentication and a stable API surface for reading and updating application records without embedding direct database credentials in the client.

### Flow and Azure mapping
A mobile client signs in through Microsoft Entra External ID or another approved identity provider, then calls an API layer. The API validates identity and authorization, resolves the requested data operation, and accesses a backend store through managed identity. A GraphQL endpoint can be hosted as an application API or implemented with a selected Azure API product; an App Service or Functions backend can supply resolvers and Cosmos DB or Azure SQL can persist records.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The AWS source specifically combines Amplify, Cognito, AppSync GraphQL, and DynamoDB. Azure has no exact one-service substitution for that bundled developer experience; identity, schema/resolver execution, offline sync, and database behavior need separate choices. This is a conceptual backend design, not an endorsement of a particular mobile SDK or an assumption of offline synchronization.

Source: [AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/patterns/build-a-serverless-react-native-mobile-app-by-using-aws-amplify.html).

entries.title: Private file access through an API and private object-storage path
entries.summary: Corporate users request controlled file access through an API while data traffic remains on private paths to object storage.

reference.title: Set up private access to an Amazon S3 bucket through a VPC endpoint
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; source-specific custom-domain technique is not reproduced as an Azure feature claim.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
An enterprise needs an internal file exchange path that avoids exposing object downloads through a generally reachable public storage endpoint.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Corporate users resolve an internal application endpoint and authenticate to an API. The API authorizes the requested object operation and returns a short-lived access mechanism or streams the content itself. The backend reaches Azure Blob Storage through private networking and private endpoints; private DNS and storage access policies constrain the path. Separate upload and download operations can use different controls.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The AWS pattern relies on an internal load balancer, API Gateway, Lambda, a VPC endpoint, and a special presigned-URL/domain arrangement. Azure SAS URL behavior and private endpoint DNS are not identical; whether a client can reach the private storage route must be verified for the actual network. Avoid placing bearer links in logs, and choose between proxying bytes and delegated access based on governance and throughput requirements.

Source: [AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/patterns/set-up-private-access-to-an-amazon-s3-bucket-through-a-vpc-endpoint.html).

nodes.technology: Microsoft Entra ID and storage RBAC

caveats: The source's internal presigned URL/domain pattern has AWS-specific details; Azure private endpoint DNS and SAS behavior require validation.

entries.title: Operational record changes streamed into an analytics lake
entries.summary: Database item changes flow through a durable stream and transformation stage to object storage for downstream analytics.

reference.title: Deliver DynamoDB records to Amazon S3 using Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose with AWS CDK
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; no AWS code, diagram, or wording copied.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Analytics consumers need a near-real-time history of changes from an operational database without repeatedly scanning the primary tables.

### Flow and Azure mapping
An application writes records to an operational store. A database change feed or CDC connector publishes change events to Azure Event Hubs. A transformation consumer validates the event envelope, normalizes fields, and writes partitioned files to Azure Data Lake Storage. Fabric, Azure Databricks, or another approved query engine can consume the lake data for dashboards, audit, and modeling. Keep the primary transactional write path separate from its analytics copy.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The AWS example uses DynamoDB change capture, Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose, and Lambda conversion. Azure Cosmos DB change feed is not a drop-in equivalent for DynamoDB Streams, and Event Hubs plus an ingestion consumer must be designed for ordering, retries, schema evolution, duplicates, and checkpointing. The diagram is an Azure adaptation of the data movement idea, not a promise of identical consistency or delivery semantics.

Source: [AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/patterns/deliver-dynamodb-records-to-amazon-s3-using-kinesis-data-streams-and-amazon-data-firehose-with-aws-cdk.html).

reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; this entry abstracts the pattern and does not reproduce the source implementation.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Operators need searchable, timely telemetry from event-driven application functions, with useful views for troubleshooting and service health.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Functions emit structured logs and metrics to Azure Monitor through supported instrumentation or a collector. Diagnostic settings and data collection rules route selected records to Log Analytics or an Azure Data Explorer workspace. Workbooks or dashboards let operators correlate requests, dependencies, and failures. A separate export path can deliver governed records to an external observability platform if required.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The AWS source uses a Lambda Telemetry API extension to send telemetry directly to OpenSearch, bypassing its default log intermediary. Azure Monitor is the natural Azure-native baseline, but not a direct OpenSearch substitute; high-cardinality data, retention, sampling, ingestion volume, and query costs need sizing. Avoid routing every verbose trace or sensitive payload into long-retention logs. The graph is an observability pattern, not an application architecture.

Source: [AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/patterns/send-telemetry-data-from-lambda-to-opensearch-for-analytics-visualization.html).

entries.summary: A control-plane router assigns tenants to isolated cells, stores mappings, tracks capacity, and returns stable tenant endpoints.

reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; AWS explicitly states the demo/code is explanatory and not production-ready.

supporting_sources.title: Journey to Cloud-Native Architecture Series #7: Using Containers and Cell-based design for higher resiliency and efficiency
supporting_sources.relevance: Adds first-party implementation context for lightweight routing, cell isolation, tenant mapping, and shuffle sharding; the Azure diagram does not claim AWS topology or implementation parity.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A multi-tenant service may need to assign newly registered tenants to bounded workload cells and avoid routing every request through a central control plane.

### Flow and Azure mapping
A client authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID and calls a placement API. The control plane looks up or assigns a tenant-to-cell mapping in a metadata store, checks recorded capacity, and returns a stable cell endpoint. Tenant workload traffic then goes directly to that cell through Azure Front Door or API Management. A queue-driven provisioning workflow can request additional cells, while monitoring tracks cell health and occupancy.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
This is not the existing generic Deployment Stamps starter: the focus is tenant placement, static endpoint mapping, and independent control-plane availability. Azure Deployment Stamps can host cells, but the routing and placement logic remains workload-specific. The AWS reference is explicitly a demonstration, not production-ready. Assignment races, tenant migration, capacity definitions, endpoint caching, authentication continuity, and outage recovery need separate engineering.

Source: [AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/patterns/serverless-cell-router-architecture.html).
caveats: The source says the demo is not production-ready; provisioned cells and tenant-migration mechanics are outside its detailed scope.

entries.title: Industrial edge-to-cloud data backbone for operational insights
entries.summary: Layered ingestion, edge buffering, cloud data management, and analytics support operational use cases across industrial sites.

reference.title: Phase 3: Defining a blueprint — Building an industrial Internet of Things digital transformation strategy
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; source gives functional layers rather than a prescriptive Azure service mapping.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Industrial organizations need a repeatable, modular way to collect IT/OT data at multiple facilities, preserve local operation during connectivity interruptions, and make selected data useful to cloud analytics teams.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Sensors, PLCs, historians, MES, and enterprise systems feed a site ingestion layer. Azure IoT Operations or a site gateway can normalize and buffer data locally; Azure Arc provides management where applicable. A secure site-to-cloud connection forwards selected telemetry to Azure Event Hubs or Data Lake Storage. Fabric, Azure Data Explorer, or Databricks supports analytics and downstream business applications. Identity, patching, logging, and configuration management are cross-cutting responsibilities.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The source is a functional blueprint, not a concrete AWS service diagram. Azure service choices are explicit adaptation proposals. Local autonomy, data residency, semantic models, buffering limits, and industrial protocol support vary by site. Don't overstate edge operation during disconnection or imply a single cloud platform covers PLC control and safety functions.

Source: [AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-iiot-transformation/phase-3.html).
caveats: The source is conceptual and names no single prescribed service topology; local buffering, control, and protocols must be validated.

entries.title: Multi-region read-local, write-primary application resilience
entries.summary: Regional application stacks serve local reads while a designated primary accepts writes and replicates data asynchronously to a recovery region.

reference.title: Multi-Region fundamental 2: Understanding the data
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; design principles are paraphrased, with no AWS diagram reused.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A workload needs regional availability for read-heavy traffic while accepting that cross-region data replication is asynchronous and recovery may require reconciliation.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Global traffic routing sends users to a healthy regional application endpoint. Reads can use local replicas or caches; writes are directed to a selected primary data region. Azure SQL geo-replication or a selected Cosmos DB multi-region configuration may be considered only after confirming the workload's consistency and conflict requirements. A failover procedure changes routing and validates the data state; event replay or reconciliation handles in-flight work.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The source stresses that asynchronous replication can create stale reads and missing or in-flight writes after failure, and that applications often need changes for failover, idempotency, and reconciliation. Azure Cosmos DB and SQL geo-replication have different semantics; neither should be labeled a generic replacement for DynamoDB Global Tables or Aurora. No RTO/RPO or consistency guarantee is claimed.

Source: [AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/aws-multi-region-fundamentals/fundamental-2.html).

nodes.label: Global traffic routing
nodes.technology: Azure Front Door or Traffic Manager

caveats: Consistency and failover behavior are database-specific; asynchronous replication can lose or delay unreplicated writes.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
An enterprise wants to make governed data reusable across operational producers, analytics teams, and business consumers without forcing every workload into a single storage or query engine.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Batch and streaming producers land data in Azure Data Lake Storage or OneLake. Azure Data Factory, Event Hubs, and stream processing services feed and transform the data. A catalog and governance layer classifies data and coordinates access; curated datasets are served through Fabric Warehouse, Azure Data Explorer, Azure AI Search, or purpose-built stores. BI and ML consumers use approved interfaces. Select only components relevant to a particular implementation.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The AWS guide is a broad architecture overview, not a single deployable topology. The Azure graph is intentionally a composable platform pattern, and services such as Lake Formation, Glue, Redshift, OpenSearch, and Kinesis do not map one-to-one to Azure products. Data ownership, encryption, consent/privacy, retention, lineage, and quality are organizational practices as well as service settings.

Source: [AWS Prescriptive Guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-aws-data/aws-architecture.html).

entries.title: Global application with regional front ends and a single-region Azure SQL writer
entries.summary: Global ingress routes to regional application tiers, while writes go to a single Azure SQL primary and a secondary receives asynchronous geo-replication.

reference.title: Global deployment with Compute Engine and Spanner
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; no Google architecture image or prose copied.

supporting_sources.title: Uncomplicating the complex: How Spanner simplifies microservices-based architectures
supporting_sources.relevance: Provides Google-side context on Spanner's relational and replication properties and trade-offs, making the non-equivalence of the Azure SQL adaptation explicit.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A global audience needs regional application entry points and a recovery design, but the Azure target must not imply the source database's globally synchronous relational semantics.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Azure Front Door routes users to regional web and application tiers. Route all writes to one Azure SQL primary region. If local reads in a secondary region are needed, use a configured geo-secondary only for workloads that tolerate replication lag; otherwise route reads to the primary. Azure SQL geo-replication is asynchronous, so the secondary is not a globally consistent writable peer. On a regional failure, an operator or tested recovery workflow promotes the secondary and redirects writes according to the chosen recovery process.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Google source uses regional application tiers with multi-region Spanner, which provides a capability this Azure SQL topology does not preserve. This adaptation **loses synchronous cross-region strong relational consistency and active-active multi-region writes**: secondary reads can be stale, and recent writes may not have replicated at failover. Azure SQL is not a Spanner equivalent. If the workload requires globally consistent relational transactions, this candidate is not a fit; evaluate a different data model or managed database design and document its actual guarantees. No RTO, RPO, latency, or zero-data-loss claim is made.

Source: [Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/global-deployment-compute-engine-spanner).

edges.label: read and write in primary region

caveats: This Azure target does not preserve Spanner's globally synchronous relational consistency or multi-region write behavior. Secondary reads can be stale, and failover can have nonzero data loss; verify current Azure SQL geo-replication behavior and workload requirements.

entries.title: Cloud recovery site for an on-premises application

reference.title: Google Cloud hybrid deployment archetype
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; source pattern is paraphrased and adapted to Azure.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A business-critical on-premises application needs a recovery location without moving its primary operation immediately to a cloud-only model.

### Flow and Azure mapping
The on-premises workload periodically backs up or replicates selected data over a secured connection to Azure. Azure Backup, Azure Site Recovery, or application-native replication may protect different components. A warm or cold Azure application environment is prepared according to recovery objectives; an operator activates the recovery workflow and updates traffic routing after validating dependencies and data state.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Google source explicitly says recovery frequency and active/passive state depend on RTO and RPO, and notes that hybrid systems require reliable secure networking and added operational effort. Azure Site Recovery is not a universal substitute for database-native consistency or application-specific recovery. The catalog should show activation as an operator-controlled step and should not imply failover is automatic or that a tested RTO is known.

Source: [Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/deployment-archetypes/hybrid).

nodes.label: Backup or replication service
nodes.technology: Azure Backup or Azure Site Recovery (workload-dependent)

caveats: Product and recovery workflow must be selected by workload; no RTO/RPO, replication mode, or automatic failover is asserted.

reference.title: RAG infrastructure for generative AI using Agent Platform and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; provider-specific architecture is not copied.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
An organization wants an assistant to answer questions using its own current documents and to measure whether generated responses are relevant and grounded.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Upload events trigger document processing. A pipeline extracts text, chunks content, creates embeddings, and indexes records in Azure AI Search. At request time, an application retrieves relevant chunks, packages context with the user question, calls a selected Azure model endpoint, applies response checks, and returns a response. An offline evaluation path stores prompts and response ratings for review and regression tests.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Google source separates ingestion, serving, evaluation, and databases, and uses an AlloyDB pgvector store. Azure AI Search is a different retrieval service, not an equivalent database extension; index configuration, filtering, hybrid retrieval, embedding compatibility, and data lifecycle need separate choices. Evaluation does not guarantee factual answers, and document access controls must be enforced during retrieval.

Source: [Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/rag-capable-gen-ai-app-using-vertex-ai).
caveats: Evaluation logs can contain sensitive prompts and responses; apply retention and access controls.

reference.title: Deploy a secured serverless architecture using Cloud Run functions
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; source blueprint controls are paraphrased, not copied.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A background action should run in response to a storage or messaging event and reach an internal service without exposing the function or its dependencies as public endpoints.

### Flow and Azure mapping
A private storage upload or event source emits a notification to Event Grid or Service Bus. An Azure Function consumes the event using a managed identity and connects through private networking to the target data service. Secrets belong in Key Vault; network egress is limited and monitored. Separate development, test, and production environments use isolated resource scopes and controlled release paths.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Google blueprint uses Shared VPC, VPC Service Controls, Cloud KMS, Secret Manager, and Cloud Run functions. Azure Functions, Private Link, managed identity, Key Vault, and networking policies are conceptual counterparts, not feature parity claims. Exact trigger types and private reachability depend on the Azure service integration. Keep retries, poison-message handling, idempotency, and outbound allowlists visible in detailed diagrams.

Source: [Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/blueprints/serverless-functions-blueprint).
caveats: The exact private endpoint, trigger, and secret integration are service-dependent; the source's Google controls are not Azure controls.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Repeated model retraining needs consistent data validation, training and evaluation, reproducible artifacts, and a controlled route to online serving.

### Flow and Azure mapping
A data arrival or schedule triggers an Azure Machine Learning pipeline. It validates input data, transforms features, trains a candidate, evaluates it against criteria, and registers a versioned artifact. A release pipeline promotes a passing version into an inference environment such as managed online endpoints or AKS. Monitoring captures model and service signals and can inform future retraining decisions.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Google source distinguishes continuous training on new data from CI/CD deployment of a changed pipeline implementation. Azure ML Pipelines and registries are candidates for the same responsibilities, but pipeline semantics and artifact formats differ. A promotion gate should not be implied to guarantee fairness, accuracy, or drift absence; the team must define measurable thresholds and human review where appropriate.

Source: [Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/architecture-for-mlops-using-tfx-kubeflow-pipelines-and-cloud-build?hl=en).

reference.title: Build an ML vision analytics solution with Dataflow and Cloud Vision API
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; uses the source's flow concept without copying diagrams or prose.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Organizations need to enrich large collections of user- or device-submitted images with machine-readable annotations for search, reporting, or downstream models.

### Flow and Azure mapping
A client uploads an image to Blob Storage. Event Grid notifies a queue or processing function. A scalable worker invokes an approved image-analysis model or computer-vision service, stores annotations and processing metadata in a structured analytics destination, and emits status for retries and review. Data can be queried with Fabric or Azure Data Explorer, subject to the selected data shape.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Google source uses Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, Dataflow, Vision API, and BigQuery. Azure AI Vision and Azure analytics services are adaptation choices, not guaranteed equivalent feature sets. Input scanning, content rights, privacy, unsupported media, request quotas, asynchronous batch support, and cost per image must be evaluated. Avoid depicting face recognition or sensitive classification unless a policy review and specific use case justify it.

Source: [Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/building-a-vision-analytics-solution).

reference.title: Enterprise application blueprint architecture
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; Google blueprint is used as design evidence only.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
A platform team needs consistent application delivery across development, non-production, and production, while isolating tenant workloads and operating regional clusters.

### Flow and Azure mapping
A build pipeline creates immutable container images and promotes them through environments. Azure Kubernetes Service clusters in separate environments and regions host tenant namespaces. Azure Front Door or an application gateway routes external traffic; an internal service mesh or Kubernetes service discovery handles service communication. Entra workload identities, Azure Container Registry, Azure Policy, and Azure Monitor provide candidate identity, artifact, governance, and operations layers.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
This is a specialized multi-tenant platform blueprint, not a generic AKS baseline or a single application microservices diagram. Azure AKS Fleet Manager and service mesh choices need validation for current capabilities and operational model. Namespace-level separation alone is not a complete security boundary; per-tenant data resources, authorization, network controls, environment separation, and cluster failure domains must be selected deliberately.

Source: [Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/blueprints/enterprise-application-blueprint/architecture).

nodes.label: Workload identity and policy

caveats: Multi-cluster tenancy and tenant data isolation need dedicated design; namespaces do not alone guarantee hard isolation.

reference.title: Stream logs from Google Cloud to Splunk
reference.source_terms: Not independently verified; Splunk is shown only as a generic external log analytics destination in the Azure adaptation.

entries.explanation_md:
### Problem
Centralized log export can fail transiently when a downstream analytics platform is unavailable or throttles requests; operators need buffering and a controlled recovery path.

### Flow and Azure mapping
Azure Monitor diagnostic settings and Log Analytics export routes send selected records to Event Hubs. A stream-processing or worker layer enriches and forwards events to an external HTTP collector. A secondary queue or storage-backed dead-letter path retains failed messages for investigation and replay. Managed identity or a protected Key Vault secret authenticates outbound delivery; private networking and egress allowlists constrain access.

### Trade-offs and assumptions
The Google reference uses an organization-level aggregated logging sink, Pub/Sub, a primary Dataflow-to-Splunk pipeline, and a secondary replay pipeline. Azure Monitor, Event Hubs, and Functions/Stream Analytics are not exact behavioral equivalents. Delivery guarantees, retention, ordering, duplicate handling, payload limits, and downstream acknowledgments need explicit decisions. Avoid collecting sensitive fields unless classification and redaction are in place.

Source: [Google Cloud Architecture Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/stream-logs-from-google-cloud-to-splunk).
